title: Magnify test parallelism with display voltage-imaging retention maps
idea: Repurpose the non-contact voltage-imaging testers used on LCD backplanes, where an electro-optic modulator reads millions of pixel voltages at once, to image every memory cell's stored-voltage decay through a test-mode electrode layer. The result is a cell-exact retention map per panel in minutes.
why: Fact 3: gives erasure decoding and targeted refresh complete weak-cell maps at near-zero test cost, versus hours of ATE time for silicon DRAM.

title: Apoptotic rows: autonomous self-test and soft repair during self-refresh
idea: Cells that detect their own damage trigger programmed death (apoptosis). During self-refresh, an on-die BIST samples rows at extended retention. Rows that fail retire themselves and swap in spare rows through soft-PPR registers, which persist in a small OTP block. The die reports the swaps to the host through mode registers.
why: The die heals VRT and aging failures in the field without host ECC escalation. Factory retention test time can shrink (test cost), and fewer DUEs reach the host.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM routes around defects via on-wafer mesh
idea: Scale jump (die -> wafer): keep the 300 mm wafer whole, stitch reticles with a fault-tolerant mesh NoC, and at bring-up disable defective reticle tiles in software. Dicing, packaging and per-die yield loss disappear, so a die-killing defect costs one tile.
why: Usable-bit yield approaches ~95% vs ~80-85% die yield; also removes package/TSV cost and gives ~TB/s internal bandwidth.

title: CERN trigger-buffer logic: declared-lifetime rows skip refresh entirely
idea: LHC trigger buffers hold data for microseconds and discard 99.99% of it, so nobody refreshes them. Add a NOREF(range, lifetime) command: the OS or runtime marks rows whose data will be overwritten or discarded within ~30 ms (activations, framebuffers, network rings, attention scratch), and the DRAM leaves them out of internal refresh. Reading a row past its declared lifetime returns a poison flag.
why: In AI workloads a large share of the footprint is short-lived. Skipping its refresh cuts refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) in proportion, and lets those regions use weak-retention cells (fact 3).

title: Wafer-sibling weak-cell maps predict faults across a fleet
idea: Po: a die inherits its siblings' diseases. Every DIMM uploads in-field error and weak-row logs keyed by wafer lot and die (x,y); a fleet database learns spatial signatures such as edge-ring capacitor bowing and pushes predicted weak rows to sibling dies' controllers, which boost refresh on those rows or retire them before the first error.
why: Reliability without guard-band: vendors ship with less margin and hyperscalers cut uncorrectable errors by an estimated 30-50%, turning marginal dies into sellable parts.

title: Under-hood automotive: phase-change heat spreaders clip DIMM thermal spikes
idea: Automotive ECUs ride out engine heat soak with thermal mass. Fill DIMM and HBM heat spreaders with a phase-change material that melts near 80 C (paraffin blend or Ga-In-Sn alloy), so it absorbs workload bursts and keeps DRAM under the 85 C point where retention halves and 2x refresh kicks in.
why: Avoids doubled refresh (bandwidth and energy) and retention-tail failures during bursts, and lets marginal retention bins operate safely (fact 3).

title: Child's time-out corner: quarantine hammering rows in a spaced subarray
idea: A child who keeps poking siblings is sent to the time-out corner: once a row's activation count spikes, the controller moves that aggressor's data into a quarantine subarray where every other row is an empty guard row, so the row can be hammered without disturbing anyone.
why: Fact 9: protects against hammer thresholds down to ~1k activations at about one subarray's capacity cost.

title: TLC-NAND strategy: relaxed-window DRAM on idle trailing DRAM lines
idea: Adapted from the NAND industry's move to TLC/QLC, which accepted far worse raw cells because controllers could correct them: older 2x/1x-nm DRAM lines run with loosened process windows (fewer capacitor rework loops, short retention screens, minimal fuse repair) to produce raw-grade dies sold only into ECC-heavy CXL controllers.
why: Capital intensity and supply (fact 4): idle or fully depreciated trailing DRAM capacity becomes productive; relaxed screens and repair raise yield and throughput 10-20% and cut test cost, feeding a cheap controller-corrected tier.

title: Fishing zones and quotas: tenant-exclusive subarrays with boundary ACT limits
idea: Fisheries combine exclusive economic zones with catch quotas instead of tracking each fish. The FPGA/CXL controller gives each tenant (VM/ASID) exclusive subarray zones, so hammering inside a zone harms only its owner. Only boundary rows, about 1-2% of all rows, carry small ACT counters with strict quotas.
why: Cross-tenant hammer protection with ~50x less tracking SRAM, and it scales to thresholds of ~100 (fact 9). It needs only controller logic and kernel allocation.

title: Sleep biologist: printed TFT banks rest under reverse bias to undo drift
idea: A biologist knows brains need sleep to clear damage: printed oxide and organic TFTs suffer bias-stress threshold shift, so the controller rotates banks of a printed memory foil into 'sleep' (data migrated out, gates held at reverse bias, optionally lit by a printed OLED backplane) to detrap charge and restore Vth before the bank rejoins.
why: Bias-stress drift is the main reliability killer of printed TFTs; scheduled recovery could stretch usable life ~10x and keep sense margins without replacing the foil.

title: Substitute refresh timer with same-process canary cells that flip first
idea: Swap the fixed 64 ms refresh clock for a few deliberately undersized 'canary' capacitors per subarray, built in the same litho/etch steps so they track the local leakage tail and temperature; when a canary flips (checked by a cheap read every few ms), only that subarray is refreshed.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3): most subarrays hold data 4-10x longer than the worst-case guard band, so canary gating cuts refresh energy/bandwidth loss 60-80% and lets tail-limited dies pass bin.

title: Magnify the ECC codeword to an entire 8 KB DRAM row
idea: Every activation already latches the whole 8 KB row into the sense amps, so a row-wide quasi-cyclic LDPC decoder (~3% parity) in the bank periphery corrects the full row at activation/restore instead of using 128-bit SEC words. Raw BER up to ~1e-3 becomes acceptable versus ~1e-6 today.
why: Facts 1 and 8: turns 128x overfetch into a free ECC window; weaker cells are fine, so Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~2.5 fF (AR ~35:1 instead of 70:1) for ~3% parity overhead.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: panel-fab memory sold by good-gigabyte
idea: Build oxide-TFT DRAM on Gen-8 glass panels with existing display tools, all at <=400 C. Tile it into ~1 cm2 tiles, each with its own tile router, and map dead tiles at test. Modules are sold by the panel's verified good capacity, and software only ever sees good tiles.
why: Panel fabs cost far less per m2 than a DRAM fab and need no EUV; tolerating 20-30% dead tiles makes their defect density viable, for perhaps 3-5x lower capital per bit at relaxed density (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Variable-pitch hammer-hardened row zone for page tables and kernels
idea: TRIZ separation by condition: each bank has a ~3% zone laid out at wider wordline pitch with larger capacitors on the same U.S. process; the OS places page tables, kernel and security metadata there while the dense 6F2 zone holds ordinary data with lighter mitigation.
why: Hammer attacks that matter (privilege escalation) hit the hardened zone, so the dense zone can accept lower thresholds and simpler trackers; suits a trusted domestic defense supply.

title: Delay-line mode: streamed weight reads double as refresh at 115 C
idea: In mercury delay lines, data were refreshed simply by circulating. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token batch (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight reads to touch every row within its hot retention window and marks those banks refresh-exempt, with a watchdog that issues real refresh whenever traffic pauses.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): weight banks stay correct at 105-115 C, where refresh would otherwise quadruple, so memory no longer forces chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers); weight-memory refresh energy drops to ~0.

title: Substitute blocking ECC decode with speculative use of raw NV data
idea: Let the CPU consume raw NV read data immediately while a strong ECC decoder (needed for weak NV cells) checks in parallel; on a detected error the pipeline rolls back like a branch mispredict.
why: Hides 5-20 ns of strong-ECC latency so weak, cheap NV cells meet the 10-100 ns DRAM-class target.

title: Skip fab retention test; profile retention in customer racks
idea: Reverse the test order: dies ship after a short functional test, skipping the hours-long hot retention screen and burn-in; on first boot and weekly thereafter the controller runs retention-pattern sweeps during idle and bins each row into refresh classes stored in module NVRAM.
why: Test capex and cycle time cut ~30-50%; per-row refresh binning cuts refresh energy ~50-70% vs worst-case refresh.

title: Fighter-jet limp-home: weak rows twin-pair into differential 2T2C
idea: Combat aircraft fall back to a limp-home mode instead of failing outright. Rows that fail retention or hammer screening are paired with a neighbour row and sensed differentially as one true-plus-complement 2T2C row, halving their capacity but doubling signal, instead of using up spare rows or scrapping the die. Pairing is set per row by fuse or runtime register.
why: Spare rows run out first on weak dies. Twin-pairing rescues dies with many weak rows and lets fabs run thinner capacitors with selective rescue: several points of yield (facts 1, 3).

title: Paraffin phase-change lid keeps stacks under 85 C
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: a sealed U.S.-made paraffin/fatty-acid phase-change pack bonded to the memory-stack lid melts at ~70 C, absorbing AI burst heat so DRAM never enters the 85 C+ double-refresh range, and refreezes between bursts.
why: Avoids the 2x refresh rate and retention-fail spikes during bursts (~10-15% bandwidth recovered at peak) and lets retention-marginal dies pass, using domestic petrochemical material.

title: Eliminate weak-cell errors by storing safe states: data inversion masks
idea: True cells fail only from charged to discharged, and anti-cells only the reverse. The controller keeps a weak-cell map and, for each 64-bit word, picks one of 4 XOR masks so every known weak cell stores its non-decaying state. The 2-bit mask index replaces some ECC bits.
why: Eliminates most retention-tail failures without shortening refresh; could double the refresh interval at <3% overhead.

title: EnerJ approximate storage fixed with age-aware asymmetric soft decoding
idea: EnerJ-style approximate storage never caught on because developers had to annotate types and accept silent errors. Fix: no refresh at all for buffers with a declared lifetime (activations, gradients, KV blocks); each write is time-stamped, and the decoder feeds elapsed age and the known 1-to-0 leakage direction as soft priors into an LDPC decode, recovering data exactly until the age limit.
why: Zero refresh power with exact, not approximate, results for data living under ~1 s, saving 16-33% of idle power (fact 3) and admitting weaker cells.

title: Hot-air rework refurbishes failed DIMMs at chip granularity
idea: Ideal: no DRAM chip is ever wasted. Closest: decommissioned and failed server DIMMs pass through 1990s-era BGA rework stations and memory testers; the single faulty package is swapped for a harvested good one and the module is re-certified with a lower-speed or extra-scrub profile.
why: Supply: returns ~70-80% of failed DIMMs to service (most failures are one chip), adding capacity at a fraction of new cost.

title: Seismograph sensor measuring actual substrate disturbance, not activation counts
idea: Seismographs measure real ground motion rather than predicting it. Each subarray gets a well-tap sense resistor and an integrator that measures the minority-carrier/substrate charge actually injected by wordline toggling and long row-open times. When the integrated charge near a region passes a calibrated fraction of Cs*dV, targeted refresh fires.
why: Mitigation then responds to physics instead of a counter proxy, so it catches RowPress and many-sided patterns (fact 9). Refresh spent on false alarms could fall about 50%.

title: Hyperscale error fingerprints: a CVE-style exchange for DRAM failure signatures
idea: The largest fleets log billions of DIMM-hours. Create an industry exchange where operators and vendors share anonymized correctable-error spatial fingerprints (bank, row and column patterns per die lot). Host controllers use them to predict which pages will go uncorrectable and retire them early, and vendors adjust screening by lot.
why: Predictive retirement makes dies with higher raw error rates safe to deploy and could cut DIMM replacements ~30-50%, lifting usable supply and tightening yield feedback to fabs (facts 3, 9).

title: Cavendish NEMS memory's stiction killer turned into the latching mechanism
idea: Cavendish Kinetics' NEMS memory pivoted away because cantilevers stuck unpredictably (stiction). Fix: design for controlled stiction, using a self-assembled monolayer that sets adhesion energy inside a narrow window so a beam latched to the 'on' contact stays put unpowered, while a counter-electrode pulse plus the beam's spring force releases it reliably.
why: Mechanically bistable: zero refresh, no leakage tail, immune to radiation and row hammer, BEOL-buildable over CMOS with no capacitor.

title: Eliminate memory ECC for tensors: algorithm-based checksums ride along
idea: Append Huang-Abraham row and column checksum vectors to every weight and activation matrix stored in DRAM. The GEMM computes its output checksums as a byproduct, so a mismatch locates and corrects a corrupted element in place, and the DRAM itself carries no ECC.
why: Recovers ECC capacity and controller energy for >80% of AI memory traffic; ~1-3% checksum overhead vs 12.5% parity, allowing cheaper ECC-free dies.

title: Multi-beam e-beam writes per-die personalized repair wiring
idea: No EUV: after wafer sort, a multi-beam e-beam writer exposes one custom upper-metal layer per die that physically reroutes around defective subarrays and bitlines, instead of using fuse banks.
why: Removes fuse/redundancy periphery area (part of the ~49% periphery tax) and gives finer-grained repair than spare rows.

title: Flight-recorder DIMM interposer capturing command history before each error
idea: An aircraft's black box records the minutes before an incident. An FPGA DIMM interposer (two board spins, about $250k) keeps a rolling 1-second ring buffer of ACT/REF commands and temperature. On any corrected or uncorrected ECC event it freezes and dumps the buffer. Deployed on ~200 partner servers within the $1M, it would build the first large dataset linking real flips to real access patterns.
why: Measured distributions of hammer and retention tails, rather than worst-case assumptions, allow right-sized mitigation and refresh margins, possibly a 2x relaxation (facts 3 and 9).

title: Movable-type sense amplifiers: swappable spare periphery slices
idea: Gutenberg's movable type made every letter replaceable; build the sense-amp, column-decoder and local wordline-driver strips as identical slices behind a small antifuse-configured crossbar, so a failed or slow periphery slice is swapped for a spare instead of scrapping the mat, which row/column redundancy cannot fix.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) and periphery defects are mostly unrepairable today; recovering them could add an estimated 3-8 yield points on 32-64 Gb and 3D dies, lowering cost per bit.

title: Checkpoint-replay memory: training runs on lightly refreshed DRAM
idea: Combine HPC checkpoint/restart with relaxed refresh: activations and optimizer state live in DRAM refreshed at 4-8x the nominal interval, and any ECC-detected failure triggers recomputation of the affected micro-batch from the last checkpoint, which training stacks already do for node failures.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): recovers ~10-20% bandwidth and much of the 16-33% idle refresh power on training clusters and turns retention-marginal dies into usable supply.

title: Fleet-proven spec: JEDEC grade with percentile error limits and mandatory ECC
idea: Hyperscaler field studies show real DRAM errors come from a small minority of cells. Create a JEDEC grade that states retention and hammer specs as percentiles (e.g., at most 1e-6 of cells may fail at 64 ms and 85 C) and requires system ECC, instead of demanding that every cell meet the worst case.
why: The worst 1e-6 tail sets refresh and capacitor height today. Percentile specs let vendors ship dies that are now scrapped or downbinned and trim guardbands: ~5-10% yield plus capacitor relief (facts 1, 3).

title: Compression-funded ECC spends freed bytes on stronger parity
idea: No EUV: when a 64B line compresses to 48B, the controller stores 16B of extra parity in the freed space, raising correction from 1 to ~8 symbols for that line. Weak DUV arrays get strong protection without fixed overhead.
why: Allows raw BER ~10-100x higher on mature-node arrays at no capacity cost for compressible data (often >50% of lines).

title: Beehive geometry: staggered wordlines so no victim has one dominant aggressor
idea: Cells sit on a hexagonal lattice where each storage node's three nearest wordlines are distinct and roughly equidistant, so hammering any single row delivers about a third of today's coupling and a double-sided attack needs three coordinated rows.
why: Fact 9: ~2-3x higher effective hammer threshold from geometry alone, buying time for cheap mitigations.

title: Retinal lateral inhibition between sense amps cancels coupling noise
idea: Retinal neurons subtract a fraction of their neighbours' signals to sharpen edges; add weak, calibrated cross-coupling between adjacent bitline sense amplifiers that subtracts a set fraction of each neighbour's developing signal, cancelling the bitline-to-bitline capacitive coupling that grows at every pitch shrink.
why: Capacitor wall and pattern-dependent errors: coupling eats ~10-20% of sense signal at 12 nm-class pitch; cancelling it lets Cs shrink or bitlines lengthen (fewer sense amps, less of the 49% periphery).

title: Substitute digital ECC decoders with charge-sharing triple-cell majority voting
idea: Store each critical bit in three cells on one bitline and open all three wordlines at once; charge sharing gives the analog majority directly at the sense amp, so TMR correction costs one activation and no decoder logic.
why: Error tolerance with no periphery logic (fact 7): enables 3x-redundant 'golden' regions for page tables and metadata on cheap cells, cutting uncorrectable rates by orders of magnitude.

title: Bit-granular weak-cell extraction into an on-die patch SRAM
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: at wafer sort the 0.01-0.1% of cells with retention under 1 s are pulled out individually; a small per-bank address CAM plus SRAM data bits shadows them, so array refresh is set by the median cell (seconds) instead of the 13 fA tail.
why: Refresh interval 64 ms to ~1 s (16x fewer refreshes, ~15-30% idle power saved) for ~0.3% die area; Cs could drop ~20% because the tail no longer sets the spec.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si tiers for cheap 3D DRAM
idea: Po: build 3D DRAM from bad transistors. Each tier's lateral access transistors use excimer-laser-crystallized polysilicon (a display-industry process) whose grain-boundary variability gives a ~1% weak-cell tail; codewords span all tiers so a weak cell or even a poor tier is just an erasure.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): a cheap deposited transistor that is good enough at 1% BER makes 26+ tiers plausible without epitaxial Si/SiGe stacks; ~2-3x lower cost per bit at 32+ tiers if it works.

title: One flag bit: polarity coding keeps weak cells discharged
idea: Imposed limit: one extra bit per 64-bit word. Retention failures happen only when a leaky cell holds its charged state. Using a boot-time weak-cell map, the controller stores either the data or its inverse, whichever puts the known weak cells of that word in their discharged, safe state, and records the choice in the flag bit.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: most weak-cell errors are eliminated at 1.6% overhead, so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x past the weak tail.

title: Soviet salvage grade: sell retention-binned reject dies with refresh maps
idea: A Soviet engineer under embargo wastes nothing: dies that fail 64 ms retention or have a few dead subarrays are binned into 16 ms and 32 ms classes and packaged as 'salvage-grade' modules whose SPD carries a compressed per-row refresh/remap table, which an open controller-firmware specification honors.
why: Supply strategy: raises usable output by an estimated 3-8% of wafer starts with zero new fab capex.

title: Single-electron-transistor sense amp counts stored electrons directly
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A single-electron transistor with a ~2 nm Si island (charging energy well above kT at room temperature) capacitively coupled to the bitline acts as a sub-electron electrometer; its periodic current oscillation (Coulomb staircase) resolves signals of a few hundred electrons, with reference cells calibrating background-charge drift.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): the Cs requirement could drop from ~5 fF to ~0.5 fF, and heavily drooped weak cells still read correctly, removing the AR-75 capacitor.

title: Probe-free wafer-level retention soaks via on-die BIST
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution: tester-bound retention testing is replaced by on-die BIST that runs multi-hour, multi-temperature retention and hammer profiling while whole wafers sit in U.S.-built burn-in ovens on a power-only contact; results are read out later in one quick touchdown.
why: Long tail screening becomes cheap (cost scales with oven space, not ATE time), so retention bins get fine-grained and good dies run longer refresh; less dependence on tester capacity.

title: Split buried wordline turns passing gate into negative shield
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: buried-channel transistor | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: EUV + split-gate etch]. The buried wordline is split so the segment that passes beside a neighbour's storage junction becomes a separately biased shield held at about -0.4 V, so toggling the aggressor no longer gates the victim's junction (the passing-gate hammer path).
why: Fact 9: removes the dominant passing-wordline hammer mechanism physically; ~10x higher hammer threshold claimed with no refresh overhead.

title: Magnify tolerated defects: Swiss-cheese DIMMs ship bad-page maps
idea: Sell DIMMs certified to contain up to 2% bad 4 KB pages, with the bad-page list in SPD. Firmware and the OS/hypervisor exclude those pages at boot, like NAND bad-block tables.
why: Fact 4: dies with clustered defects become sellable capacity instead of scrap, adding +5-15% sellable bits per wafer at ~2% capacity cost.

title: C: carbon co-implant getters point defects at storage-node junctions
idea: Add a shallow substitutional-carbon co-implant (~1e20 cm^-3) at the storage-node contact junction; carbon traps Si interstitials and binds Fe/Cu, preventing the deep-level clusters that create trap-assisted-tunneling hotspots in the depletion region.
why: Attacks the junction-leakage share of the retention tail (fact 3) with an abundant element already used for diffusion control in logic; target 3-10x fewer tail cells at equal Cs.

title: H: hydride reservoir re-passivates hammer-aged access transistors in field
idea: Deposit a Pd-capped TiHx hydride strip in the BEOL over each bank, above a window in the SiN hydrogen barrier. A controller-scheduled maintenance pulse from on-die poly heaters (~250 C for seconds, bank taken offline) releases atomic hydrogen that diffuses to the recess-gate Si/SiO2 interface and re-caps dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and hammer stress.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) widens over life as interface traps form; periodic in-field re-passivation keeps weak-cell counts near time-zero, allowing ~2x longer refresh over product life and less test guardband.

title: Leakage-twin RC oscillator clocks each bank's refresh
idea: No EUV: build a tiny relaxation oscillator whose timing capacitor leaks through a replica access transistor drawn on the same DUV process. Its period tracks process, temperature and aging leakage directly, and it clocks refresh for its bank.
why: Refresh tracks real leakage instead of the worst-case 64 ms spec, saving an estimated 30-60% of refresh energy on wide-variation DUV silicon.

title: On-die segment cache absorbs repeat activations and caps hammering
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard | integration: 256 KB SRAM segment cache per bank group | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Recently activated 64 B segments stay in an SRAM cache beside the bank; repeat accesses hit SRAM instead of re-activating, and any row that hits the cache N times is pinned there so it can never be hammered past N.
why: Constraint: for AI/KV workloads with >80% segment reuse, average access energy ~5-10x lower; Fact 9 bounded by construction.

title: Ozone radical healing of oxygen vacancies in capacitor dielectric
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: after the ZrO2-based capacitor stack is deposited (zirconium from U.S. refiners), a low-temperature ozone/oxygen-radical anneal fills oxygen vacancies that form leakage paths through the thin dielectric in the worst pillars.
why: Cuts the capacitor contribution to the leakage tail and allows ~10% thinner dielectric (more Cs per pillar), attacking fact 1 with domestic chemistry.

title: Substitute absolute FeFET levels with rank-modulation coding
idea: Encode multi-bit data in the relative order of threshold voltages among a group of FeFET cells, not absolute levels, so uniform relaxation or depolarization after power loss does not change the stored value.
why: Density: enables 2-3 bits/cell NV storage robust to drift, ~2x cost-per-bit gain without strict level placement.

title: Eliminate the fixed wordline-low rail: deep-negative bias for hammered victims
idea: Give each local wordline driver a selectable off-rail (about -0.2 V normally, -0.6 V as a shield). The controller's activation tracker switches rows next to a heavily activated aggressor to the deeper negative bias until their next refresh. That raises the barrier against hammer-induced electron injection and passing-gate leakage.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): could raise the victim flip threshold several-fold without extra mitigation refreshes, recovering their bandwidth; costs one rail switch per local driver.

title: Sub-ambient coolant loop priced against Arrhenius refresh savings
idea: Tail leakage has Ea ~0.6-0.9 eV, so retention doubles every ~8-10 C, and dropping junctions from 85 C to 25 C buys ~60-100x retention. Route 10 C facility water to the memory cold plates first, and let on-die sensors stretch refresh to 1-4 s.
why: Refresh (fact 3): recovers the 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth spent on refresh, and lets weaker binned dies pass.

title: Run the array at 0.6 V and let BCH clean up
idea: Worse: hold VARY at ~1 V because every cell must sense perfectly. Flip: drop array voltage to ~0.6 V, accept raw BER near 1e-6, and add a strong 8-bit-correcting BCH per 512-bit line in the controller, so the energy saved on bitline swings exceeds the added decode energy.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: array CV^2 energy falls ~64% and sense/restore power drops, for ~5% parity overhead.

title: Resonant-tunneling diode pair makes each storage node self-restoring
idea: Effect: negative differential resistance in resonant tunneling. Each storage node is tied to a series pair of Si/SiGe RTDs stacked above the capacitor (a Goto pair), creating two stable node voltages; leakage only nudges the node and the NDR latch pulls it back, so data holds with no periodic refresh while a sub-pA standby current flows.
why: Retention tail and refresh (fact 3): refresh-free DRAM removes ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy and 10-20% bandwidth; 1e10 cells x 1 pA is only ~10 mA standby.

title: Soft-decision sensing lets 1.5 fF capacitors meet target BER
idea: First-principles budget: bitline kT/C noise is only ~0.3 mV against ~100 mV of signal, so most of today's 5 fF of charge is spent on worst-case sense-amp offset and not on thermal noise. Sense each bitline with three staggered trip points (2-bit soft output) and feed log-likelihoods to a rate-0.94 LDPC over 1 KB, letting Cs drop to ~1.5 fF.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~20:1, which removes deep-etch and high-k steps, for ~15-20% lower cost per bit.

title: Eliminate ECC from the critical path: speculative data use with rollback
idea: Forward raw data to the core immediately and run a much stronger, slower code (2-symbol RS or LDPC over 256 B) in parallel. A detected error squashes dependent instructions, as a branch mispredict does, and replays them with corrected data.
why: Lets vendors ship cells with 10-100x higher raw BER (weaker capacitors, lower VARY) at zero average latency cost; ~10-20% cost per bit from relaxed cell specs.

title: Rows switch to twin-cell mode when HF-free cleans leave leaky cells
idea: Rearrange two single cells into one differential cell on demand: wafers cleaned without HF (ozone water, SC1/SC2, H2 bake) show more leaky-tail cells, so at boot the controller switches only rows containing tail cells into 2T2C mode, pairing them with a neighbor row storing the complement on BL/BLB.
why: Differential pairs tolerate ~10x more leakage; applied to only ~1-3% of rows, capacity loss stays small while enabling a fully HF-free front end.

title: Post-hammer neighbor de-trap pulse cancels injected charge
idea: Po: hammering heals the victim. After each aggressor precharge, the row decoder drives both adjacent wordlines ~0.3 V below the normal negative standby level for ~2 ns, sweeping carriers trapped or injected near the victim storage-node junction back to the substrate before they neutralize stored charge.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the trap-assisted electron-migration mechanism directly; claimed 5-10x higher flip threshold with no counter tables, at the cost of one extra negative-rail pulse per ACT.

title: Immune memory: VRT suspects remembered forever via controller Bloom filter
idea: Variable-retention-time cells toggle good/bad and evade one-shot profiling; any address that ever yields a correctable error enters a counting Bloom filter (the 'memory T-cells'), and rows holding suspects get permanent 2x refresh or a stronger code.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: neutralizes VRT, the main reason profile-guided refresh is distrusted, unlocking safe 4x+ refresh relaxation.

title: Bonded local sense amps per 32 cells rescue tiny capacitors
idea: Box [medium: 1 fF capacitor | access: vertical channel | sense: one sense amp per 32-cell bitline on a bonded logic wafer | integration: hybrid bonding at 0.5 um pitch | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Bitline capacitance drops ~16x, so a 1 fF cell gives more signal than a 5 fF cell does today while each sense event only charges a tiny bitline.
why: Constraint: ~10x lower bitline energy per access; Fact 1: capacitor aspect ratio can fall from ~70:1 to ~15:1, and weak cells gain margin.

title: Minify hammer aim: re-keyed row permutation every refresh window
idea: Each subarray maps logical to physical rows through a 16-bit keyed Feistel permutation. During refresh the controller re-keys one subarray per window and migrates its rows with in-DRAM RowClone, so a hammering pattern loses its physical neighbors within ~64 ms.
why: Fact 9: an attacker must land ~1k activations on unknown, moving neighbors, which turns targeted hammering into diffuse disturbance that normal refresh covers, at ~1-2% bandwidth cost.

title: Magnify the die to a whole panel; mesh routes around defects
idea: Never dice: pattern a glass panel as ~10,000 memory tiles joined by a redundant mesh and served as many channels from edge connectors. A panel-level test writes a defect map, and the router fabric bypasses dead tiles, as in wafer-scale processors.
why: Facts 4 and 7: display-fab defect densities stop mattering, and per-die dicing, packaging and known-good-die test disappear; usable panel yield nears 100%.

title: Recombination barrier implant stops hammer electrons between wordlines
idea: Inverts 'the substrate is a passive bystander': one implant mask places a deep p+ or carbon-rich trap layer between adjacent buried wordlines so electrons injected from the aggressor channel recombine before reaching the victim storage node.
why: Raises the row-hammer threshold (fact 9) from ~1k to ~10k+ activations, shrinking mitigation SRAM and extra refresh; one implant mask.

title: Incremental-redundancy reads fetch extra parity only on failure
idea: Po: memory that talks like a cellular radio. Each line carries a short fast-path BCH; extra parity for a much stronger code sits in a separate row and is fetched HARQ-style only when the short decoder fails (a few % of reads at 1% BER).
why: Holds average access latency near the 10-100 ns DRAM class while guaranteeing 1%-BER correction; average latency penalty ~5-8%.

title: Bonsai pruning: planned capacity shrink retires weakest rows yearly
idea: Instead of every cell meeting 10 years at 125 C at fab, the module ships with a declared pruning curve and asks the OS (CXL/ACPI hot-remove) to offline its weakest ~0.5% of rows per year based on in-field aging data, under a contractual capacity schedule.
why: Admits cheaper, less over-designed dies with ~5% yield/density gain while still guaranteeing function across the 10-year 125 C mission.

title: B-grade DRAM tier: buy JEDEC rejects, run them at 4x refresh
idea: Combine die binning with hyperscaler memory tiering: dies failing 64 ms retention but passing 16 ms are sold at a discount on modules whose controller profile sets 4x refresh and stronger ECC, deployed as a capacity tier for caching and inference KV-cache.
why: Usable supply and cost/bit: recovers a few percent of wafer output now scrapped or down-binned, at a tolerable bandwidth loss in capacity-bound tiers.

title: Eliminate the front-end fab: US BEOL-only lines deposit memory on bought logic
idea: Buy finished mature-node CMOS logic wafers (including from U.S. foundries) and deposit memory tiers on them in retrofitted U.S. BEOL-only lines (MEMS, packaging or display fabs) that never exceed 400 C. On-die ECC and remap in the purchased logic absorb those lines' higher defect density.
why: Cuts new-capacity capital ~5x vs a DRAM fab and time-to-capacity to ~18 months, raising U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.

title: Grid fault-current limiters islanding shorted wordlines per mat
idea: Adapted from power grids that use fault-current limiters and islanding so one short does not black out a region: each mat's local wordline-driver supply has a self-tripping current limiter (a small overcurrent-sensing latch), so a WL-to-BL or WL-to-plate short isolates its own mat instead of collapsing VPP for the whole bank; the mat is then marked out and its addresses remapped.
why: Yield (facts 4, 7): hard shorts are among the few defects that kill whole banks or dies; islanding turns a die-killer into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield on large-die parts by several percent.

title: Dead-die HBM stacks: GPU remaps around dead channels, stacks still ship
idea: Treat HBM stacking yield as the extreme case. A stack with one defective die is normally scrapped after the costly stacking step. Instead, sell it as a 7/8-capacity part: its SPD-style descriptor lists the dead die's pseudo-channels, and the GPU memory controller compacts its address map around them over the unchanged HBM interface.
why: HBM stacking yield loss of 20-30% is mostly wasted good silicon (fact 6). Recovering even half of single-die-defect stacks raises effective HBM supply by ~10%.

title: Metallized-film self-healing: clearing pulses isolate pinholes in dry-processed capacitors
idea: Bosch's 1930s metallized-paper capacitors healed themselves when a breakdown arc vaporized the thin electrode around the flaw. The DRAM capacitor's top electrode becomes an ultrathin segmented TiN film, and at wafer sort a controlled overvoltage clearing pulse drives current through any pinhole hard enough to oxidize the electrode locally, turning a shorted or leaky capacitor into a slightly smaller good one.
why: Water: capacitor modules cleaned dry (no wet cleans after high-aspect-ratio etch or between high-k layers) carry more particles and pinholes; self-clearing restores yield and the retention tail, enabling the all-dry ~10x water cut at a Cs loss of ~2-5% on healed cells.

title: Kirchhoff current-sum parity check scrubs eight rows per read
idea: Gain-cell reads are non-destructive current sources. Opening 8 read wordlines on one bitline sums their currents, and a small ADC returns that column's Hamming weight across 8 rows. Its LSB is checked against a stored column parity.
why: Capacitorless reliability: 8x less scrub energy and bandwidth, so weak cells can be checked often enough.

title: Magnify nanotube count per transistor to average away leakage variance
idea: Build each access transistor from ~20 aligned semiconducting carbon nanotubes on quartz or glass instead of 1-3. Per-device variance falls ~1/sqrt(N), and any metallic tube is burned open by an electrical breakdown pulse at test.
why: Facts 3 and 4: CNT variability blocks CNT memory; averaging plus burn-off gives a low-temperature, non-silicon access device whose leakage tail approaches the 13 fA spec.

title: KV cache at one-third cost: range-clamp decoding in gray memory
idea: Imposed limit: KV-cache memory must cost a third as much. The KV cache is stored in gray memory, meaning DRAM run at a 4x refresh interval and low VARY. Instead of parity, per-head statistics (min/max norms) are stored, and any value read outside its head's range is clamped. Attention softmax is robust to sparse bounded flips.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh and array energy for the KV cache drop 3-4x, and higher-BER binned dies can serve LLM inference.

title: Factory-seconds grade: sell retention-weak dies as inference memory
idea: Like garment 'seconds', create a product grade for dies that fail the 64 ms/85C retention spec or exceed repair, sold with a qualified controller profile (32 ms refresh, page-retirement list, on-module strong ECC) for AI inference and caches where data is rewritten constantly.
why: Turns scrap (several % of output, more on new 3D nodes) into immediate supply, raising usable bits per wafer with no capex (scarcity, cost per bit).

title: Minify charged cells with per-burst data-inversion coset flags
idea: Store 1-3 coset bits per 64-byte burst and, at write time, pick the inversion/coset that leaves the fewest cells in the charged, leakage-vulnerable state, accounting for true-cell versus anti-cell layout.
why: Fact 3: zero-heavy real data ends up mostly discharged, cutting exposed cells ~25-50%, so refresh can stretch ~1.5-2x (random data gains little).

title: Thymic negative selection: random detectors that never match normal traffic
idea: The thymus deletes T-cells that react to self; at boot the controller generates thousands of random detector templates over (bank, row-delta, ACT-interval) features, deletes any that match the profiled benign workload, and keeps survivors in a tiny CAM, so traffic that triggers a survivor is flagged as non-self and throttled.
why: Row hammer: catches novel patterns (half-double, many-sided) without per-row counters, ~10x less SRAM than counter trackers with tunable false-positive rate.

title: OLED-demura-style e-beam charge-decay imaging of leaky junctions inline
idea: OLED fabs photograph every panel to build a per-pixel compensation map. Before the capacitor is built, the storage-node contacts would be flood-charged with an e-beam and voltage-contrast imaged twice, seconds apart. Contacts that lose contrast quickly mark leaky junction outliers across the wafer in parallel. Those coordinates feed process learning and are written into die fuse maps.
why: This attacks the leakage tail (fact 3) at its source, and the faster yield learning cuts retention-test cost. It could catch the worst ~0.01% of cells before the capacitor modules are spent on them.

title: Eliminate the hard sense decision: latch resolve time as confidence
idea: Measure how long each sense amplifier takes to resolve, using a per-column time-to-digital stamp; metastability time scales as log(1/dV). Slow-resolving bits are marked low-confidence and fed as soft information to a soft-decision LDPC/BCH decoder.
why: Soft decoding gains ~2 dB of margin, enough to run VARY ~20-30% lower (fact 10, ~40% less CV2 energy) or accept smaller Cs, with no extra reads.

title: Pointer residues: self-healing data structures on unprotected memory
idea: Ideal: data structures that heal themselves. Closest: runtimes put a 16-bit residue code of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits and keep redundant back-links, so a corrupted pointer is detected on dereference and rebuilt from its partner; it runs on 1990s-class CPUs with no new silicon.
why: Fact 3: protects the control state that makes bit flips fatal, so bulk memory can run without ECC or at relaxed refresh.

title: Minimum-equipment-list grading: ship partial-good dies with signed fault maps
idea: Airliners dispatch legally with documented inoperative equipment. Draft a JEDEC-style SPD extension that carries a signed fault map (dead mats, weak rows). Write reference BIOS and CXL firmware that route around the mapped faults, and pilot 100 modules built from partial-good dies that are scrapped today. All of it fits in $1M.
why: Effective die yield up 5-15% at advanced nodes means more sellable bits per wafer and lower capital per bit (fact 4).

title: One block implant makes the access transistor asymmetric
idea: Inverts 'access transistors are symmetric': the single added mask blocks the bitline side so a low-dose counter-doping implant grades only the storage-node junction, lowering the peak field that drives GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling where the leakage tail originates.
why: Tail leakage 3-10x lower (fact 3) for ~4x longer refresh, cutting refresh's 16-33% idle power with one non-EUV implant mask.

title: N+1 hot-spare die in U.S.-assembled memory stacks
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: every domestically assembled 8-high stack carries a ninth die; base-die BIST tracks per-die error rates and, when one degrades, migrates its contents in the background and switches its channel to the spare.
why: Stack yield and field life no longer hinge on the worst of 8 dies; recovers part of the 20-30% stacking yield loss (fact 6) and permits more aggressive cell designs.

title: HPC algorithm-based fault tolerance for AI weight matrices
idea: Adapted from ABFT in scientific computing, where matrices carry row and column checksums so errors are found from the math itself: weights are stored with one checksum row and column per 128x128 tile, verified as a side effect of each matmul (output checksum vs checksum-vector product), and corrected by locating the intersecting failing row and column; DRAM ECC is turned off for those regions.
why: Capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6): ~1.5% checksum overhead replaces 12.5% ECC, freeing ~11% HBM capacity and allowing lower-grade stacks, with no hardware change.

title: Engineered damage sites that getter metals away from cells
idea: Inverts 'defects are always bad': one mask defines implant-damage gettering zones at mat boundaries that pull Fe, Cu and Ni contaminants during later anneals away from storage-node junctions, where they would form generation centers.
why: Lowers the contaminant-driven retention tail (fact 3) and relaxes purity specs on chemicals and crucibles (resource chokepoints) at constant refresh.

title: Castle moat: storage node on buried insulator removes hot junction leakage
idea: The storage contact lands on a local buried-insulator island (silicon-on-nothing or lateral overgrowth), so the storage node has no p-n junction volume in the substrate and only the access channel can leak.
why: Junction SRH generation dominates the tail at 125 C; removing it cuts hot tail leakage ~5-10x, keeping standard refresh viable for 10 years.

title: Carbon-implant proximity gettering beneath bonded array tiers
idea: Gettering is the fab's filter press; implant carbon (not argon or xenon pre-amorphisation) a few microns beneath each bonded or layer-transferred array tier, creating sinks that pull Fe, Ni and Cu out of storage-node junctions during low-temperature anneals.
why: Metal contamination is a prime source of retention-tail junction leakage, worse in low-thermal-budget 3D flows (facts 2, 3); image sensors cut dark current ~10x this way.

title: Analog leaky integrator capacitor counts hammers per row
idea: Box [medium: per-row MOS integrator capacitor | access: charge-packet injection on each ACT | sense: threshold comparator | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Every activation dumps a fixed charge packet onto a tiny per-row integrator that leaks with a time constant matched to the refresh window; crossing threshold triggers neighbour refresh, giving an exact per-row counter for about one cell's area.
why: Fact 9: deterministic tracking at hammer thresholds of 1k and below with <1% area, versus 5-10% for SRAM counter tables.

title: Cicada primes: prime-stride randomized TRR sampling defeats synchronized hammering
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime cycles to dodge predator sync; TRR samplers use reseeded pseudo-random prime-length windows (e.g. 61/67/71 ACTs) so many-sided patterns that phase-lock to fixed sampling intervals cannot align with the blind spots.
why: Fact 9: restores in-DRAM TRR effectiveness at ~zero area, deferring costly per-row counters by a node or two.

title: Unidirectional error codes matched to one-way charge leakage
idea: Retention physics is one-way: a charged node can only lose electrons, so true-cells fail 1->0 and anti-cells fail 0->1, never the reverse. After de-scrambling cell polarity, apply Bose-Lin/Borden t-unidirectional-error-correcting codes. They need far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH for the same t.
why: Retention tail/ECC overhead: parity drops from 6.25% to ~3%, or 2x the correction at equal overhead, which allows longer refresh.

title: Rewritable on-die remap CAM for lifetime self-retirement
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: replace one-shot antifuse post-package repair with an SRAM remap CAM loaded from a small rewritable on-die store and backed by a 1-2% hidden row reserve, so the scrubber retires rows as they begin failing, SSD bad-block style, an unlimited number of times.
why: Cells ship with less aging margin because degradation is absorbed in the field; ~10-20% retention guardband reclaimed as smaller Cs or longer refresh.

title: MEMS-style post-package trimming of sense-amplifier offsets
idea: MEMS gyros and oscillators are trimmed after packaging to cancel fabrication asymmetry. Each sense-amp pair gets a 3-bit capacitor-DAC trim. Final test sweeps it, and the codes go into a compact on-die OTP array, removing the systematic offset that sets worst-case signal margin.
why: Cutting SA offset sigma from ~15-25 mV to ~5 mV lets the cell signal fall ~30%: a smaller Cs (fact 1) or a weaker transistor. The trim area is small next to periphery at ~49% of the die (fact 7).

title: Coral colony tiers: build 120 monolithic tiers, keep the best 100
idea: A coral colony thrives though individual polyps die; deposit ~120 monolithic oxide-semiconductor memory tiers by low-temperature ALD/sputter with shared vertical wordline contacts, test each tier after deposition, and permanently bypass dead tiers with tier-select transistors, so ~85% tier yield still yields a full stack.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers to break even; at ~100 EUV-free tiers cost per GB falls ~30-100x, and tier sparing removes the compound-yield wall (0.99^100) that kills deep stacks.

title: Multi-reference soft sensing lets a 2 fF capacitor work
idea: Po: the capacitor is too small to matter. Each sense amp compares the bitline against three staggered references in one sensing window (time-multiplexed offset injection), emitting a hard bit plus a confidence flag; low-confidence bits go to the decoder as erasures, so cells with half the signal still read correctly.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~2-2.5 fF, so pillar AR falls from ~70:1 toward ~35:1 and the hardest etch steps go away.

title: Adaptive-infill ECC: code strength varies page by page
idea: 3D printers vary infill density where stress is high; classify every 4 KB page at test and in the field by measured weakness and store it with a matching code rate (none, SEC-DED, or ~12% BCH), tracked in a page-attribute table, so strong pages hand their parity bits back as capacity.
why: Uniform worst-case ECC wastes ~12.5% of bits; adaptive rate recovers ~6-9% capacity on typical dies while still tolerating weak tails (cost per bit).

title: Grid protective relays isolating shorted mats at runtime
idea: Power grids open relays to isolate faulted segments and keep the rest live. Each mat's VPP/VBLP feed gets a tiny current monitor and pass gate. A wordline-bitline or capacitor short drawing excess current trips isolation for that mat alone, and its addresses remap to a spare mat. Today such a short kills the bank or the die.
why: Shorts are a top yield killer on large dies, so this could add ~3-8% yield. It also makes the die resilient to hard shorts that appear in the field.

title: Ti: titanium-airframe damage tolerance schedules DIMM replacement from error growth
idea: Borrowing aerospace titanium inspection logic (Paris-law crack growth), fleet software fits each DIMM's correctable-error growth curve and predicts time to first uncorrectable error, scheduling replacement or regrading at planned maintenance.
why: Keeps weaker modules safely in service longer and avoids crashes; cuts premature replacements ~30%.

title: Tensor checksums replace DRAM ECC for model weights
idea: Flip error checking from memory to compute: weight matrices carry row/column checksums (algorithm-based fault tolerance), the GEMM verifies them, and a mismatch re-fetches that tile from a peer GPU or flash; the weight region in DRAM drops ECC entirely.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC overhead for AI's largest data class and tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER weak cells; checksum cost <1% of FLOPs.

title: Crossbar parity mats: a 2D product code built into geometry
idea: Ideal: error correction as part of the array geometry, with no decoder. Closest: each 180 nm mat reserves one parity row and one parity column maintained by XOR trees in the sense-amp and column stripes, so any single bad cell sits at the intersection of a failing row parity and a failing column parity and is flipped back.
why: Facts 1 and 3: corrects isolated weak cells at ~3% overhead with trivial logic, allowing relaxed cell specs.

title: Erasure-coded subarrays give on-die chipkill at 3x defect density
idea: Die yield follows exp(-A*D0). Spare rows fix point defects, but one dead subarray or sense-amp stripe kills the die. Stripe each access across 18 subarrays as RS(18,16) symbols, so any two dead subarrays are erased by fuse map.
why: Yield/capital: die yield ~60% to ~90% at the same D0, so fabs can ship from less mature, cheaper tools and ramp faster. Costs 12.5% of bits.

title: Mat-location-tuned ECC strength map from fail-bit statistics
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: mats at array edges, next to sense-amp stripes or on known litho hotspots borrow spare columns to run a t=2-3 BCH code while interior mats keep SEC; the strength map is fused at sort from fail-bit-map statistics.
why: Spends parity only where errors cluster: ~30-40% less total parity at equal FIT, or 10x higher raw BER tolerated in hotspot mats, raising yield of aggressive cells.
